title: Design Bitset
description:
# Design Bitset

A bitset stores a fixed number of bits indexed from `0` to `size - 1`. Initially every bit is `0`.

Implement the `Bitset` class:

* `Bitset(int size)` initializes a bitset with `size` zero bits.
* `void fix(int idx)` sets the bit at index `idx` to `1`. If it is already `1`, nothing changes.
* `void unfix(int idx)` sets the bit at index `idx` to `0`. If it is already `0`, nothing changes.
* `void flip()` changes every `0` to `1` and every `1` to `0`.
* `boolean all()` returns whether every bit is currently `1`.
* `boolean one()` returns whether at least one bit is currently `1`.
* `int count()` returns the number of bits currently set to `1`.
* `String toString()` returns the current bitset as a string whose character at index `i` is the current value of bit `i`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["Bitset", "fix", "fix", "flip", "all", "unfix", "flip", "one", "unfix", "count", "toString"]
[[5], [3], [1], [], [], [0], [], [], [0], [], []]

**Output:**
[null, null, null, null, false, null, null, true, null, 2, "01010"]

**Explanation:**
`Bitset bs = new Bitset(5)` starts as `"00000"`.
`fix(3)` gives `"00010"`, then `fix(1)` gives `"01010"`.
`flip()` gives `"10101"`, so `all()` is `false`.
`unfix(0)` gives `"00101"`; another `flip()` gives `"11010"`.
`one()` is `true`. After `unfix(0)`, the bitset is `"01010"`, so `count()` is `2` and `toString()` returns `"01010"`.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= size <= 10^5`
* `0 <= idx < size`
* At most `10^5` total calls will be made to `fix`, `unfix`, `flip`, `all`, `one`, `count`, and `toString`.
* At most `5` calls will be made to `toString`.
* At most `5` calls will be made to `all`.

solutions.name: Dual Char Views with Flip Flag
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) for updates and queries, O(n) for toString
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store two character arrays: one for the normal view and one for the flipped view. A boolean flag decides which array is currently visible. Single-index updates write both arrays at the same index so either view stays ready.

## Key Insight

`flip()` becomes O(1) because it only swaps the visible interpretation and changes `ones` to `size - ones`. The cost is duplicating the string view so `toString()` can return the active array directly.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) for `fix`, `unfix`, `flip`, `all`, `one`, and `count`; O(n) for `toString`.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Raw Boolean Array with XOR Flag
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) for updates and queries, O(n) for toString
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store raw boolean bits and a global `flipped` flag. The logical value at index `i` is `raw[i] ^ flipped`. To set a logical one or zero, write the raw value that will evaluate correctly under the current flag.

## Key Insight

The stored value and the logical value are different after a flip. Every point update must assign `raw[idx] = !flipped` for a logical one and `raw[idx] = flipped` for a logical zero, otherwise repeated flips corrupt the count.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) for updates and aggregate queries; O(n) for `toString`.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Java BitSet with Global Flip Flag
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) for updates and queries, O(n) for toString
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use Java's `BitSet` as compact raw storage and keep the same global flip flag and `ones` counter. `fix` and `unfix` write the raw bit needed for the requested logical value.

## Key Insight

`BitSet` reduces memory compared with a boolean array, but it does not remove the need for a logical flip layer. The aggregate count is still maintained manually so `count`, `all`, and `one` stay O(1).

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) for point updates and aggregate queries; O(n) for `toString`.
- Space Complexity: O(n) bits plus object overhead.

solutions.name: Complementary Ones and Zeros Sets
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) average for updates and queries, O(n) for toString
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain two sets: indexes currently equal to one and indexes currently equal to zero. `fix` moves an index from `zeros` to `ones`, `unfix` moves it back, and `flip` swaps the two set references.

## Key Insight

This route models the bitset as two complementary partitions. Global flip is just exchanging the partitions, so it avoids a special raw/logical conversion in point updates.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) average for `fix`, `unfix`, `flip`, `all`, `one`, and `count`; O(n) for `toString`.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Lazy Segment Tree with Range Flip
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) for updates, O(1) for count/all/one, O(n) for toString
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat `flip()` as a range flip over the whole interval and `fix` or `unfix` as a point assignment. A segment tree stores the number of ones in each interval and a lazy flip bit for pending range inversions.

## Key Insight

This is more general than the specialized flip-flag solution: it teaches the invariant behind lazy propagation. Flipping an interval changes its one count to `length - ones`, and the lazy flag remembers that children still need the same inversion.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n) for `fix` and `unfix`, O(1) for `flip`, `all`, `one`, and `count`, O(n) for `toString`.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

tests.description: Canonical example with flip, all, one, count, toString, and updates after a flip.
Lazy flip must keep all, one, count, and toString consistent after fixes.
Single-bit boundary covers all and one transitions through fix, flip, and idempotent unfix.
Repeated fix and repeated unfix must not double-count or underflow the number of ones.
After a global flip, unfix and fix must update logical values instead of raw stored bits.
Double flip restores the original state, then all bits fixed and flipped to zero update all aggregate queries.
Multiple toString calls around updates catch stale cached-string implementations.
Alternating bits across several indexes exercise toString order and logical writes under a flip flag.
